The Civil Rights Movement. Primarily from the nineteen fifties to nineteen sixties, though it had roots in earlier decades and continuing effects, this was the sustained campaign by African Americans and allies to end racial segregation and discrimination in American law and society. Led by figures like Martin Luther King Junior and Malcolm X, it employed nonviolence, civil disobedience, litigation, and political pressure to challenge Jim Crow laws, desegregate institutions, and win voting rights, transforming American law, politics, and culture, though structural racism and inequality persist.

The movement had deep roots as the NAACP, founded in nineteen oh-nine, challenged segregation through litigation. A. Philip Randolph organized the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom in nineteen forty-one to demand integrated defense industries. The nineteen fifties saw mounting legal and political challenges to segregation. Plessy v. Ferguson in eighteen ninety-six had enshrined separate but equal as constitutional law, but the landmark Brown v. Board of Education decision in nineteen fifty-four declared segregation in schools unconstitutional, though enforcement would be slow and fiercely resisted.

The Montgomery Bus Boycott from nineteen fifty-five to nineteen fifty-six, sparked by Rosa Parks' refusal to give up her seat to a white passenger, lasted three hundred eighty-one days and ended bus segregation. Martin Luther King Junior, a young minister, emerged as a national leader of nonviolent resistance.

King's strategy drew on Mahatma Gandhi's philosophy of satyagraha, truth force. The movement employed sit-ins where students refused service at segregated lunch counters, freedom rides of mixed-race buses challenging segregation in interstate travel, and marches to confront segregation directly. The March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom on August twenty-eighth, nineteen sixty-three drew two hundred fifty thousand people to the Lincoln Memorial. King's "I Have a Dream" speech became the movement's most iconic articulation, imagining a nation where people are judged by content of character not color. The Selma to Montgomery marches in March nineteen sixty-five protested voting discrimination. The violent police response, Bloody Sunday on March seventh, nineteen sixty-five, when state troopers attacked marchers, shocked Americans and catalyzed federal action on voting rights.

The Civil Rights Act of nineteen sixty-four, passed under President Lyndon B. Johnson, prohibited discrimination in public accommodations, employment, and education and was the broadest civil rights legislation since Reconstruction from eighteen sixty-five to eighteen seventy-seven. The Voting Rights Act of nineteen sixty-five suspended literacy tests and authorized federal election monitors in jurisdictions with histories of discriminatory voting. It had immediate impact in the South, where Black voter registration surged. The Fair Housing Act in nineteen sixty-eight prohibited discrimination in housing sales and rentals, completing the legislative trilogy of nineteen sixties civil rights law and passed days after King's assassination.

By the mid-nineteen sixties, the movement fragmented. While King pursued legislative gains and nonviolence, more radical figures including Malcolm X, James Carmichael, and Huey Newton advocated Black Power, self-determination, pride in black culture, and willingness to defend against violence. Malcolm X, a spokesperson for the Nation of Islam until nineteen sixty-four, criticized King's integration goals and nonviolence as accommodationist. His assassination on February twenty-first, nineteen sixty-five shocked the nation and left the movement's philosophical direction contested.

Urban uprisings in Watts in nineteen sixty-five and Newark and Detroit in nineteen sixty-seven, along with post-King assassination uprisings in nineteen sixty-eight, reflected Black anger at continuing poverty and police brutality even as civil rights laws passed. The Kerner Commission in nineteen sixty-eight documented systemic racism and inequality.

The movement transformed American consciousness about race as it redefined Black identity from shame to pride. Soul music, black studies programs, and African American cultural assertion flourished as expressions of Black power and dignity. The movement inspired other social movements including the women's liberation movement, Chicano rights, Native American activism, and LGBTQ plus rights, adopting the movement's tactics and moral framework of equality and dignity. The movement won concrete legal and political gains including desegregation of schools, though de facto segregation persisted, integration of public accommodations, expanded Black political representation as the number of Black elected officials surged, and expanded civil rights protections.

Legally, the civil rights laws of the nineteen sixties transformed American society as courts struck down remaining Jim Crow statutes, schools and workplaces integrated unevenly, and Black political participation grew. Yet structural racism persisted as de facto segregation through housing discrimination, redlining, and white flight maintained residential separation, wealth gaps remained vast, and police brutality continued to disproportionately target Black Americans.
